'''Allan Roth''' (born '''Abraham Roth'''; May 17, 1917 – March 3, 1992) was a Canadian baseball and hockey [[statistician]] and an early proponent of [[sabermetrics]] in baseball. During his career, Roth worked for the [[Los Angeles Dodgers|Brooklyn/Los Angeles Dodgers]] as their official statistician from 1947 to 1964.

Roth is considered by many to be the father of modern [[sabermetrics]]. He was the first full-time statistician ever employed by a [[Major League Baseball]] team, creating a number of new baseball statistics over the course of his work.

==Early life==
Roth was born in [[Montreal, Quebec]] to Jewish immigrants Rose (née Silverheart) and Nathan Roth. He was second of three children, born after his older brother Max and his younger sister Sylvia.<ref name=sabr-roth>{{cite web |title=Allan Roth (SABR BioProject) |url=https://sabr.org/bioproj/person/Allan-Roth/ |work=Society for American Baseball Research}}</ref>

Roth attended Strathcona Academy and, in his free time, compiled statistics for his hometown [[Montreal Royals]] of the [[International League]]. Additionally, he also compiled hockey statistics. He attended and graduated from [[McGill University]]. He would legally change his name from "Abraham" to "Allan" in 1941.<ref name=sabr-roth/>

In 1941, Roth was hired by [[Frank Calder]], president of the [[National Hockey League]], as the official statistician of the league after he showed Calder his compiled hockey statistics. This came after he tried to find a job with [[Larry MacPhail]], the [[general manager (baseball)|general manager]] of the [[Brooklyn Dodgers]], who was uninterested in Roth's work.<ref name=sabr-roth/>

Three months after his work with the NHL began, however, Roth was drafted into the [[Canadian Army]]. He worked in the unit charged with organizing reinforcement contingents for Canadian Forces in Europe, where he managed all the records and statistics. In January 1944, he was discharged from the Army due to [[epilepsy]]. After being discharged, he began to write articles in the sports section of the ''[[Montreal Standard]]'' and compiled statistics for the [[Montreal Canadiens]].<ref name=sabr-roth/>

In 1944, Roth met with [[Branch Rickey]], who had replaced MacPhail as the general manager of the Dodgers, sending him a four-page letter contained proposals to track a wide range of statistics. Rickey was impressed with Roth's work and offered him a job with the Dodgers. However, visa issues after [[World War II]] prevented Roth from taking up his new position until 1947.<ref name=sabr-roth/>

==Baseball career==
Upon taking up his new position, Roth proceeded to break down statistics into various categories such as performance against left-handers and right-handers, in the various ballparks, in situations [[Scoring position#Batting average with runners in scoring position|with runners in scoring position]], and performance in different [[Count (baseball)|ball-strike counts]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Brown |first1=Daniel |title=Homage to stats freaks |url=https://www.espn.in/mlb/news/story?id=1836155 |work=[[ESPN]] |date=July 8, 2004}}</ref> At the end of each season, he would compile the numbers on each player, including his newer, advanced stats. He also spent the next eighteen seasons [[pitch count|recording every pitch thrown]] in a Dodgers game as well as their outcome.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Maher |first1=Charles |title=Baseball Game of Figures for Dodger Statistician |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times-allan-roth-profile/64237512/ |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=August 11, 1963}}</ref>

After Rickey departed from the Dodgers, new owner [[Walter O'Malley]] moved Roth to the press and public relations operation. As a result, his analyses and statistics began to appear regularly in the newspaper columns. Roth ran a publication called ''Press Box Pickups'', which contained his work as well as promotional material and was distributed in the press box during gamedays. He was also put in charge of providing statistics for the team's yearbooks and [[media guide|media guides]].<ref name=sabr-roth/>

Initially working from behind home plate, Roth was moved to the radio booth in 1954 where he provided statistics and facts to broadcasters. He quickly struck up a friendship with Dodgers broadcaster [[Vin Scully]]. From the booth, Roth also got a link to the press box and often provided statistics and analyses to reporters for their stories.<ref name=":0">{{cite news |last1=Scully |first1=Vin |title=From Early On, Allan Roth was the Man Behind the Numbers |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/03/22/sports/backtalk-from-early-on-allan-roth-was-man-behind-numbers.html |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=March 22, 1992}}</ref>

After the Dodgers moved to [[Los Angeles]], Roth began to attend spring training in [[Vero Beach, Florida]]. He began to meet up with each player and would evaluate their performance from the previous year, emphasizing their strengths and weaknesses and suggesting changes to help the player improve their performance. Future [[National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum|Hall of Fame]] pitcher [[Sandy Koufax]] credited Roth with helping him turn around his career through these sessions.<ref name=sabr-roth/>

Roth is credited with inventing [[on-base percentage]] and showing how it was more important than [[Batting average (baseball)|batting average]]. He also created an early version of [[save (baseball)|saves]] for [[relief pitchers]] in 1951. The save was adopted in 1964 and became an official statistic in 1969, both times with the help of [[Jerome Holtzman]] and with a slightly different formula than that of Roth's.<ref name=sabr-roth/>

Roth was fired by the Dodgers during the 1964 season after it was discovered that he was having an extramarital affair with an [[African-American]] woman, when the two had a fight in the corridor of a Philadelphia hotel. O'Malley disliked controversy and, as [[interracial relationships]] were frowned upon at the time, the press were told that Roth had resigned because he was tired of travelling. The real reason was revealed decades later by [[Buzzie Bavasi]], Dodgers' general manager in the 1960s, in a 1994 interview.<ref name=sabr-roth/>

Roth continued to contribute to baseball afterwards, writing articles for ''[[The Sporting News]]'' and editing ''Who's Who in Baseball''. Roth also contributed statistical data for Sandy Koufax's autobiography, ''Koufax''. In 1966, he was hired by [[NBC Sports|NBC]] to provide statistical data to broadcasters [[Curt Gowdy]] and [[Tony Kubek]] for the [[MLB on NBC|Game of the Week]], [[Major League Baseball All-Star Game|All-Star Games]] and the [[World Series]]. A few years later, he moved to [[ESPN on ABC|ABC]] and provided the same service. Roth retired in the 1980s due to ill health.<ref name=sabr-roth/>

===Legacy===

For his contributions to baseball, he was elected to the [[Canadian Baseball Hall of Fame]] in 2010.<ref>{{cite web |title=Canadian Baseball Hall of Fame |url=https://www.baseball-almanac.com/hof/hofcana.shtml |website=Baseball Almanac}}</ref> Statistician [[Bill James]] wrote that Roth "was decades ahead of his time" and was the person who "started it all" when it came to baseball statistical analysis.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |date=2022-02-15 |title=Long Reads: Allan Roth: The story of the Canadian who was MLB's first team statistician |url=https://cooperstownersincanada.com/2022/02/15/long-reads-allan-roth-the-story-of-the-canadian-who-was-mlbs-first-team-statistician/ |access-date=2025-03-10 |website=Cooperstowners in Canada |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="sabr-roth" /> He was praised by [[Vin Scully]] and sportswriters [[Alan Schwarz]] and [[Dick Young (sportswriter)|Dick Young]] for his groundbreaking statistical analyses.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Schwarz |first=Alan |url=https://archive.org/details/numbersgamebaseb00schw |title=The numbers game : baseball's lifelong fascination with statistics |date=2004 |publisher=New York : T. Dunne Books |others= |isbn=978-0-312-32222-9 |via=Internet Archive}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Jenks |first=Jayson |date=November 7, 2019 |title=The outsider’s advantage: Freedom to ditch the old ways and embrace new solutions for a sport’s problems |url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/1303284/2019/11/07/the-outsiders-advantage-freedom-to-ditch-the-old-ways-and-embrace-new-solutions-for-a-sports-problems/ |access-date=2025-03-10 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

The [[Society of American Baseball Research]] (SABR) named their Los Angeles chapter, where he was often attended meetings and showed his new workings during the offseasons, in his honor. In 2019, they posthumously awarded him the [[Society of American Baseball Research#Awards|Henry Chadwick Award]] for his contributions to baseball research.<ref>{{cite web |title=SABR announces 2019 Henry Chadwick Award recipients |url=https://sabr.org/latest/sabr-announces-2019-henry-chadwick-award-recipients/ |work=Society for American Baseball Research}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Roth married Esther Machlovitch in 1940. The couple had two children: a son named Michael, and a daughter named Andrea. They divorced in 1965, one year after his affair was discovered and he was fired by the Dodgers.<ref name=sabr-roth/>

Roth died of a heart attack in Brotman Hospital in [[Culver City, California]] on March 3, 1992.<ref>{{cite news |title=Allan Roth, 74, Dies; Baseball Statistian |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/03/05/sports/alan-roth-74-dies-baseball-statistician.html |work=[[The New York Times]] |agency=Associated Press |date=March 5, 1992}}</ref>
